one_liner: Header-only C++17 constexpr minimal perfect hash for fixed integer key sets; lookups ~2.5x faster than std::unordered_map in author benchmarks.
what_it_does: Builds a minimal perfect hash over a fixed set of integral keys at compile time (or at runtime via assign()). Each key maps to a unique dense slot in [0, N), which you use to index a parallel array or drive a switch. The API is phf::make_phf(keys) returning phf::phf<T, N>, with find() (slot or phf::npos), count(), at()/operator[] (throw on miss) and an unchecked lookup(); it stores no values and has no iterators. Strings are not supported directly: you hash them to integers yourself and, for open input, compare the original string kept at the returned slot.
how_it_is_fast: It uses a two-level CHD ("hash, displace, and compress", Belazzougui/Botelho/Dietzfelbinger, ESA 2009) scheme. The key's low bits select a bucket, and the bucket's stored multiplier and offset place the key with a division-free multiply-shift, ((k * mul) >> shift) + off, into a power-of-two index table; this replaces the classic prime modulo. A lookup is therefore one mask, one multiply, one shift, two array reads and one key compare, with no probing, heap or pointer chasing, so the cost stays at about 1.2-1.3 ns from 6 to 1000 keys. The displacement search (largest buckets first, successive prime multipliers, rollback on collision) runs in constexpr, and key sets that defeat plain multiply-shift (such as distinct powers of two) fall back automatically to an xorshift-multiply pre-mix, which ARCHITECTURE.md says costs about half the multiply-shift speedup.
when_to_use: Key set known at build time and already integral (enum values, opcodes, protocol or field IDs, precomputed string hashes), from a handful to about a thousand keys, where you need key to dense index for a parallel array.
Replacing a sparse switch or if/else ladder: with a constexpr table, find(hash("...")) is a constant expression usable as a case label, so the dispatch compiles to a jump table.
Hot lookups on small fixed sets where std::unordered_map's hash-plus-probe floor (about 3.1-3.2 ns in the author's runs) matters and a flat ~1.2-1.3 ns per find() is worth a custom API.
Code that must avoid heap allocation or static-init work: a constexpr table is plain arrays in the binary, with no dependencies beyond the standard library.
String keyword dispatch where you control the hash and can add one string compare, and do not want gperf's separate code-generation step.
when_not_to_use: Keys change at runtime: there is no insert, erase or rehash, and even runtime assign() rebuilds the whole table and needs the key count N as a template parameter.

You want native string keys or mapped values out of the box: phf.hh is integer-only, the string wrapper exists only as benchmark code (bench/phf_dispatch.hh), and the `keywords` front-end that ARCHITECTURE.md and AGENTS.md point to returns 404.
Raw string-lookup speed matters most and a codegen step is acceptable: gperf ran 14 ns/op against 21 ns for phf hash+verify in this repo's own 192-keyword benchmark.

Large constexpr key sets: construction is a compile-time search, compile-time cost is not measured anywhere, and the repo only builds constexpr tables of 8 keys (test.cc, demo.cc); its 1000- and 5000-key runs use runtime assign().

You need a proven dependency: 37 stars, one closed issue, no tags or releases (README pins GIT_TAG master), and the lookup was rewritten in July 2026, with a GCC 13 constexpr fix the next day; MSVC support is not documented.

integration.dependencies: none (standard library only; <iostream> only under PHF_DEBUG). The benchmarks alone fetch frozen and ctrie.
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (CMake target sets cxx_std_17; CMake 3.14 for the FetchContent path). Commit 55ac236 reports validation on Clang, GCC 11, g++-13.4 and g++-16; g++-13.3 needed that fix for find() as a case label. MSVC not documented.
integration.platforms: any C++17 target (portable integer code, no intrinsics); published numbers are x86_64 only
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Lookups are const member functions over immutable arrays with no internal mutable state, so concurrent reads of a built table are safe by construction; assign() and clear() mutate.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — find()/count()/at() reuse std set/map names, but find() returns a dense slot index or phf::npos instead of an iterator, no values are stored, keys must be integral, and the set is fixed. Against a switch or if-ladder it replaces the comparisons, and the case labels become find(key) constants.

gotchas: Only lookup() skips the membership check. find(), count() and at() compare the stored integer key and reject non-members, despite the README's note that find() 'hands back whatever sits there'. The real risk is with strings: a non-member whose hash equals a member's hash is reported as a hit unless you compare the stored string.

Key types: the correctness suite tests only uint32_t, uint64_t and int keys. By my reading of phf.hh (not tested), 8/16-bit key types are promoted to 32-bit before the multiply, so ((k * mul) >> shift) can index past the table. Signed 64-bit keys use signed multiplication, so overflow is UB and negative results break the index. Prefer uint32_t or uint64_t.

Build failures throw std::invalid_argument (duplicate keys, empty or oversized input, 'cannot find suitable table'), and in a constexpr context these become compile errors. at() and operator[] throw std::out_of_range. A -fno-exceptions mode is not documented.

Memory is not compact: each index slot holds the key plus a size_t position (16 bytes for uint32_t keys on 64-bit targets), the index is the next power of two at or above 1.25N, and buckets add 8 bytes each. That is about 41 KB for 1000 uint32_t keys (derived from the phf.hh layout), while the benchmarks loop over a hot 4096-lookup work list.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over frozen or ConstexprCore/perfect_hash when the keys are already integers and you want dense [0, N) slots usable as constexpr case labels; for strings, those libraries take string keys natively, and gperf beat it in its own harness (14 vs 21 ns). ConstexprCore's table showing kronuz::phf at 0.22 vs its own 1.08 billion queries/s pins constexpr-phf at 2019 commit 0776e93, before the multiply-shift rewrite, so that table does not measure the current lookup.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's harness (GCC 11, -O3, x86_64 with no CPU model, libstdc++ inferred), find() on runtime-built tables of 6-1000 random uint32 keys took 1.2-1.3 ns per lookup against 3.1-3.2 ns for std::unordered_map<uint32_t,uint32_t> (~2.5x); this was an all-hit loop of independent lookups, and the 'if-ladder' and 'switch' columns are a runtime loop and std::lower_bound, not compiler-generated code. On 192 Xapiand field-type strings with a 50/50 hit/miss mix, hash+verify took 21 ns/op against 29 ns for std::unordered_map<std::string,int> and 82 ns for std::set, while gperf took 14 ns.
status_note: Active again since July 2026 (multiply-shift rewrite, GCC 13 fix, benchmarks, README) after a 2019-2026 gap; MIT-licensed, and the single ~1,500-line header (two-thirds of it a prime table) is easy to vendor, but it has a small user base and no tagged releases.
